summary: Your name beside mine: The player has a draft and goes to a colleague to ask them to sign on as co-sponsor.
realLife: One life: After years of work on a military justice bill, a Democrat and two Republicans announced a large cosponsor list that crossed the aisle, and a prosecutors' group said one Republican's support would pull more along. Another: Members who passed bills described signing up nearly a whole state delegation, or building a committee and freshman group from both parties early, and advised finding common ground first. Another: She picked a Senate companion partner because of shared issue, constituents and background, saying the partner depends on who has shown interest in the topic.
gates: The bill record shows a bill the player drafted and has not yet filed, or has filed with room for co-sponsors.
{the colleague} sits in the body and is tied to the player on the record.
{the colleague} has a stance on the bill's subject on the stance record.
weights: How close {the colleague} stands to the bill's subject.
What a favor to the player is worth to {the colleague}.
Whether {the colleague} sits in the other party or the other chamber.
Whether {committee chair} counts co-sponsors when deciding to hear the bill.
Whether the player has put a name on a bill for {the colleague}.
choices: ask plainly and say what the bill does
offer to change a part to win the name
offer your own name on their bill in return
wait until the colleague asks you

branches.then: Their name goes on the bill record, and {committee chair} weighs it when deciding whether to hear the bill.

branches.when: {the colleague} says yes if a part of the bill changes
branches.then: A bargain over the text begins; if the player agrees, the change is written and the name goes on.
The ask is kept open on the record with a day to talk again; the player's wait is read as patience or as pressure.
The refusal is written on the tie with its reason; the colleague may say it at the next vote.

branches.when: the colleague is of the other party
branches.then: A yes is read in both caucuses, and the bill gains weight with the chair and loses it with the player's own side.
